sections.h2: Ways to sell a house in Palatine
sections.html:
Three routes exist: hire a listing agent, sell it yourself, or take an offer from a cash buyer. Listing gives the widest exposure but means showings, buyer financing and repair requests after inspection. An investor paying cash will accept the property in its current condition and can set closing around your calendar, which suits a house with deferred maintenance, tenants in place, or a probate timeline.

Palatine is a mostly residential village in the northwest Chicago suburbs, mainly in Cook County with a portion in Lake County. Population was 67,908 in 2020 and is 65,842 now, about 3 percent lower. Much of the housing was built in the decades after 1950, and buyers of houses that age tend to ask about roofs, furnaces and basements first.

  • Gather the deed, the last tax bill, any permit records and the rental license if the house was leased.
  • Ask the title company which county and municipality your parcel belongs to.
  • Compare any offer to what a listed sale would net after repairs, carrying costs and fees.

Roughly two of every three Palatine homes are owner-occupied. With median rent at $1,549 and about a third of units not owner-occupied, some buyers are investors who lease houses out. An investor can price repairs into an offer, which is why an as-is sale can draw interest here.

sections.h2: Which repairs need a Palatine building permit?
sections.html:
The village issues two kinds of permit. Express covers small, listed projects on detached single-family homes, with a stated goal of review within 5 business days. Standard covers larger work, with a goal of 10 to 15 business days. The Building and Inspection Services Division at 200 E. Wood Street answers questions at 847-359-9042.

These projects need a permit:

  • Building or replacing a deck, shed, roof or fence.
  • Installing or replacing an air conditioner, furnace or water heater.
  • Finishing or remodeling a basement, kitchen or bathroom.
  • Adding or altering the electrical system, or replacing an electric stove with a gas model.
  • Drainage work, including regrading and connecting a downspout or sump pump to buried pipe.

Painting, installing flooring, replacing a faucet and swapping a window or door of the same size in the same opening usually do not. If a past owner did permit-required work without one, ask the division how to resolve it before a buyer's inspector finds it. Pull your permit records together early, because a buyer will ask for them whenever a roof, furnace or basement has been redone.

The village sits in wooded marshland where several streams begin. Most drain to Salt Creek, which rises at Wilke Marsh on the east side, while the northeast corner drains to Buffalo Creek and a small piece of the southeast to McDonald Creek. Wet basements, sump pumps and grading are therefore routine inspection topics.

If your house has had water in the basement, a buyer will want to see repair records and any permit for drainage work. Drainage work is on the permit list above, so check that it was done with one. Selling as is to a cash buyer avoids the repair negotiation, though the buyer will still price the problem into the offer.

sections.h2: What to do before you take offers
sections.html:
A little preparation shortens the sale, whichever route you choose. Start with the paperwork, because most delays in a Palatine closing trace back to a missing record, not to the house itself.

  1. Find the deed and the most recent tax bill, and note which county the bill comes from.
  2. Collect permit records for any roof, furnace, water heater, deck or basement work, and invoices for drainage or sump pump repairs.
  3. If the house was rented, locate the Rental Dwelling License and the current lease, and decide whether the tenant stays.
  4. Ask your title company to confirm the county and municipality from the parcel number.
  5. Request offers, and compare each one with what a listing would net after repairs, carrying costs and fees.

A cash buyer can usually move through this list faster because the offer does not depend on a lender's appraisal or on the buyer's inspection list. A listed sale gives you more time in the market and may bring a higher price, but expect to repair or credit what the inspector finds.

sections.h2: Does Palatine require a rental license?
sections.html:
Yes. Under Chapter 12 of the village code, every residential rental, including single-family homes, townhomes and condominiums, must be inspected and carry an annual Rental Dwelling License. The program dates to 1990.

An owner applies through the Citizen Self Service portal, pays the invoice, calls for an inspection, and attends a landlord seminar while adopting a Palatine lease addendum. The license expires one year after the application date and renews automatically unless the owner asks to close it.

If a tenant lease runs past your closing date, tell buyers whether the license is current. If an investor buys the house, the new owner starts the licensing steps for that address. Ask the village how to close your license once the sale is done.

Palatine has no village transfer tax. The taxes that remain are the state and county ones, collected at recording. The state rate is 50 cents per $500 and the county rate is 25 cents per $500. A deed for a sale needs the state transfer declaration (PTAX-203), which is filed through the state's MyDec system.

One detail trips people up. Some Palatine mailing addresses are actually in Rolling Meadows, which charges its own transfer tax. A Palatine address does not guarantee a Palatine location, so have the title company confirm the municipality from the parcel number. If your parcel sits in Lake County instead of Cook, you record with the Lake County Clerk's Recording Division.

Palatine also has a Metra station on the Union Pacific Northwest Line, and a downtown rebuilt since December 1999 with a passenger station, a parking garage, condominiums and rowhouses near the tracks. Commuting is the village's selling point, so mention the walk or drive to the station in your listing.

faqs.q: Does Palatine charge a real estate transfer tax?
faqs.a: No village transfer tax applies. Illinois and the county still collect their own transfer taxes at recording, at 50 cents per $500 for the state and 25 cents per $500 for the county.

faqs.q: Which county records a Palatine deed?
faqs.a: Most of the village is in Cook County, so the Cook County Clerk's recording office handles those parcels. A portion lies in Lake County, and those parcels are recorded by the Lake County Clerk's Recording Division. Your title company can confirm which one applies from the parcel number.

faqs.q: Is a permit needed for a new roof or water heater in Palatine?
faqs.a: Yes. Building or replacing a roof, and installing or replacing a water heater, furnace or air conditioner, all need a permit. Express review is aimed at 5 business days. Call 847-359-9042 if you are unsure about a specific job.

faqs.q: Do I have to license a Palatine house I rent out before selling?
faqs.a: If it is rented, it needs an annual Rental Dwelling License under the village's Chapter 12 program. The license lasts one year from the application date and renews automatically unless you ask to close it.

faqs.q: Will anyone buy a Palatine house that needs work?
faqs.a: Yes. Many buyers, especially investors, purchase older Palatine houses as they are. Expect a buyer to price in roof, furnace, drainage and permit issues, so gather your permit records and any repair invoices before you ask for offers.
